Workshop 5 · Sessions 16–18 · Thursday 5 November 2026

Which item matches best? Texts as vectors, cosine similarity and TF-IDF

A customer types "a cup of tea" into a café app. Counting shared words puts a cup of black coffee as high as the teas, because both start with "a cup of". Today you turn every menu item into a list of numbers, measure how alike two lists are, and give rare, telling words like tea more weight than words like a and of.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • turn a text into a vector: one count per word of the vocabulary
  • work out the cosine similarity of two vectors, by hand and in Python, and say what 1 and 0 mean
  • explain why words that appear everywhere (a, of, with) make unrelated texts look alike
  • compute IDF and TF-IDF weights, and rank items for a search query with them
  • say what TF-IDF cannot see: words that mean the same, like cold and iced

Course outcome CO2 · Reading: [SLP] Chapter 6, sections 6.3 to 6.5

Before class: pre-read

1. Checklist

  • git pull run in your ADS6703 folder, so the Workshop 5 notebook is in ADS6703/w05/
  • The Workshop 4 practice problems tried

2. Where you already meet this

Every time a computer says "these two texts are alike", something like today's method is often behind it:

  • the search box of a shop or a café app, ranking items for what you typed
  • "customers who looked at this also looked at…", from item descriptions
  • finding duplicate questions on a help forum, or similar complaints in an inbox

3. The whole idea in five minutes

A text as a list of numbers. Write down, for every word of the vocabulary, how often it appears in the text. "a cup of tea" has a 1 under a, cup, of and tea, and 0 under every other word. That list is a vector.

Cosine similarity: do two arrows point the same way? Think of each vector as an arrow. tea and tea tea point the same way: same topic, one is just longer. Cosine similarity measures that:

\[ \cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a| \times |b|} \]

The dot product a · b multiplies the two vectors number by number and adds up. The length |a| is the square root of the sum of the squares. 1 means the same direction, 0 means no shared words.

TF-IDF: rare words count for more. Search a menu for "a cup of tea" by counting shared words, and a cup of black coffee scores high, because it shares a, cup and of. Those words are on almost every item, so they tell you nothing. TF-IDF gives every word a weight:

\[ \text{tf-idf} = \text{tf} \times \log_{10} \frac{N}{\text{df}} \]

tf (term frequency) is how often the word appears in the text, shrunk with a log: 1 + log₁₀(count), or 0 if the word is not there. N is the number of texts, and df (document frequency) is how many of them contain the word. A word in every text gets weight 0; a rare word gets a big weight.

4. Read

  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 5, Embeddings: sections 5.3 (simple count-based embeddings) and 5.4 (cosine for measuring similarity).
  • [SLP] Chapter 11, Information Retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: sections 11.1.1 to 11.1.3 (documents as vectors, tf-idf, scoring a document). Skip BM25 and the rest of the chapter for now.

5. Try (optional)

Search for "cheap phone case" on any shopping site. Look at the first five results. Which words from your search do they share, and is there a result that matches the meaning but uses different words?

Handout: vectors, cosine and TF-IDF cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the lab.

Words

vocabulary every different word in the texts, in a fixed order
vector a list of numbers: one per vocabulary word
document one text: a menu item, a review, a web page
dot product multiply number by number, add up
length √(sum of the squares)
cosine similarity 1 = same direction, 0 = nothing shared
tf term frequency: how often the word appears in this text, shrunk with a log
df how many documents contain the word

Formulas

dot product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + …
length |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + …)
cosine cos(a, b) = a · b ÷ (|a| × |b|)
tf 1 + log₁₀(count), or 0 if the count is 0
idf log₁₀(N ÷ df)
tf-idf tf × idf
log₁₀ log₁₀ 1 = 0, log₁₀ 2 = 0.30, log₁₀ 4 = 0.60, log₁₀ 10 = 1

Worked example: four menu items

A a cup of green tea · B a cup of black coffee · C a glass of iced tea · D a cup of hot chocolate. Query: a cup of tea.

With counts. The query has length √4 = 2; each item has 5 words, so length √5 ≈ 2.24. With only 0s and 1s, the dot product is the number of shared words: A 4, B 3, C 3, D 3. So A ≈ 0.89, and B, C, D are all ≈ 0.67: the coffee ties with the iced tea.

With TF-IDF. Every word appears once in an item, so every tf is 1 + log₁₀ 1 = 1 and each weight is just the idf. N = 4. a, of: df 4, idf 0. cup: df 3, idf 0.12. tea: df 2, idf 0.30. Every other word: df 1, idf 0.60.

Weights Length Dot with query Cosine
query cup 0.12, tea 0.30 0.32
A cup 0.12, green 0.60, tea 0.30 0.68 0.104 0.47
C glass 0.60, iced 0.60, tea 0.30 0.90 0.09 0.31
B cup 0.12, black 0.60, coffee 0.60 0.86 0.014 0.05

The teas now come first.

Python

sorted(set(words)) the vocabulary, each word once, in order
[counts[w] for w in vocab] a text as a vector
sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)) dot product
math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) length
df.update(set(item.split())) add 1 to df for each different word of an item
1 + math.log10(c) if c > 0 else 0 tf of a word with count c
math.log10(N / df[w]) idf
